packs.title: Names that care
packs.question: What does the reading warn against?
options: Mocking others and using hurtful nicknames.
packs.explanation: The selected passage names ridicule and offensive nicknames.
packs.discussion: How could a nickname feel funny to one person and hurtful to another? Use made-up examples, without naming someone who was hurt.
packs.activity: Each person invents a kind greeting for a fictional new neighbor. Everyone may pass if they prefer.
packs.close: Choose one greeting to try together. Do not record names or personal stories.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains the warnings about ridicule, fault-finding and disliked names. The greeting exercise is an editorial application.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَكُونُوا۟ خَيْرًا مِّنْهُمْ وَلَا نِسَآءٌ مِّن نِّسَآءٍ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَكُنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهُنَّ ۖ وَلَا تَلْمِزُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا۟ بِٱلْأَلْقَـٰبِ ۖ بِئْسَ ٱلِٱسْمُ ٱلْفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ ٱلْإِيمَـٰنِ ۚ وَمَن لَّمْ يَتُبْ فَأُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّـٰلِمُونَ
passage.translation: O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), not let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames. Bad is the name of lewdness after faith. And whoso turneth not in repentance, such are evil-doers.

packs.title: A thank-you worth saying
packs.question: Who is mentioned alongside gratitude to Allah in this reading?
packs.explanation: The passage names parents and recalls a mother’s hardship.
packs.discussion: What is one ordinary kind action that is easy to overlook? You can discuss a fictional household instead of your own.
packs.activity: Make a spoken thank-you message for a caregiver. No craft materials, private story or sending a message is required.
packs.close: Each participant can say one word they want to remember.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar describes gratitude to Allah and parents. This pack does not require a child to disclose family circumstances.

passage.arabic: وَوَصَّيْنَا ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ بِوَٰلِدَيْهِ حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُۥ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ وَفِصَـٰلُهُۥ فِى عَامَيْنِ أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَٰلِدَيْكَ إِلَىَّ ٱلْمَصِيرُ
passage.translation: And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents - His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years - Give thanks unto Me and unto thy parents. Unto Me is the journeying

packs.title: The borrowed book
packs.question: What does the reading ask about entrusted things?
options: Hide them when they are damaged.
packs.explanation: The selected verse includes returning trusts to those entitled to them.
packs.discussion: A fictional class lends out books. What should happen if a borrowed book is damaged?
packs.activity: Act out a short conversation returning a fictional book and honestly explaining its condition.
packs.close: Name one action that makes a shared library easier to trust.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains returning trusts and judging fairly. The library is a fictional application.

passage.arabic: ۞ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تُؤَدُّوا۟ ٱلْأَمَـٰنَـٰتِ إِلَىٰٓ أَهْلِهَا وَإِذَا حَكَمْتُم بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ أَن تَحْكُمُوا۟ بِٱلْعَدْلِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ نِعِمَّا يَعِظُكُم بِهِۦٓ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ سَمِيعًۢا بَصِيرًا
passage.translation: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly. Lo! comely is this which Allah admonisheth you. Lo! Allah is ever Hearer, Seer.

packs.title: Pause before sharing
packs.question: What action does the reading call for when the described report arrives?
options: Assume a vivid story must be correct.
packs.explanation: The passage warns about acting on an unchecked report and harming others.
packs.discussion: A fictional message says a public event was canceled. What source would actually confirm the claim?
packs.activity: Together list the exact claim, its original source and one independent way to verify it. Use a made-up message.
packs.close: Choose a simple question to ask before forwarding.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar stresses verification before believing and passing on the described report. The message checklist is editorial applied reasoning.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَـٰلَةٍ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَـٰدِمِينَ
passage.translation: O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did.

packs.title: A fair packet
packs.question: Which contrast appears in the reading?
options: Giving and receiving the same stated amount.
Taking full measure but giving others less.
packs.explanation: The passage describes a double standard in measuring.
packs.discussion: A fictional shop promises ten counters in a bag but gives nine. Why does the label matter?
packs.activity: Use fingers or imagined counters to show a full bag and a short bag. Propose a fair correction without real shopping.
packs.close: Say one way to make a promise about quantity clear.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains short measure. The counter exercise applies that reading to an invented shop.

passage.arabic:
وَيْلٌ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ٱكْتَالُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ
وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَو وَّزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ
passage.translation:
Woe unto the defrauders:
Those who when they take the measure from mankind demand it full,
But if they measure unto them or weight for them, they cause them loss.

packs.title: A thoughtful welcome
packs.question: What does the report encourage about guests?
options: Ignore them until they bring a gift.
packs.explanation: The report pairs generous hospitality with care for neighbors and good speech.
packs.discussion: What might help a fictional guest feel included without spending money?
packs.activity: Plan a welcome using only a greeting, a place to sit and a choice to join or quietly watch.
packs.close: Everyone may choose a welcome phrase or pass.
packs.teaching: The activity is a practical suggestion inspired by the named report, not a required hospitality ritual.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018
sources.note: Abu Hurayra’s report encourages care for neighbors, hospitality and good speech.

packs.title: A strong pause
packs.question: How does the report describe strength?
packs.explanation: The report contrasts physical victory with self-control in anger.
packs.discussion: In a made-up board game, a turn feels unfair. What could a respectful pause sound like?
packs.activity: Practice a short phrase such as “I need a moment; can we check the rule?” Nobody must reenact a personal conflict.
packs.close: Choose a calm phrase to keep in mind.
packs.teaching: This communication exercise is editorial, not clinical advice or a promise that a phrase solves every conflict.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6114
sources.note: Abu Hurayra’s report describes strength as self-control in anger.

packs.title: A truthful repair
packs.question: Which habit does the report praise?
packs.explanation: The report connects truthfulness with righteousness.
packs.discussion: A fictional cup breaks. What is a truthful way to tell a grown-up without blaming someone else?
packs.activity: Take turns offering a simple honest explanation. Use imaginary events and do not handle broken objects.
packs.close: What makes an explanation clear and kind?
packs.teaching: The broken cup is a fictional practice prompt, not a test of a child’s character.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6094
sources.note: The report distinguishes habits of truthfulness from habits of lying.

packs.title: Learn one, teach one
packs.question: Which paired actions does the report praise?
options: Learning the Quran and teaching it.
packs.explanation: The report names learning and teaching the Quran together.
packs.discussion: What can you do if you do not know a reading well enough to teach it?
packs.activity: Choose a passage already known to the group, ask a capable adult to check it, and explain one clearly attributed reading detail. You may instead discuss how to find a reliable teacher.
packs.close: Say where you would check a word you are unsure about.
packs.teaching: This is a learning invitation, not a competence certificate or an automated recitation assessment.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5027
sources.note: Uthman’s report praises learning the Quran and teaching it.

packs.title: Kindness in an ordinary moment
packs.question: Which pair of actions is named in the reading?
packs.explanation: Pickthall’s translation names justice and kindness in the selected verse.
packs.discussion: A fictional group has one shared set of pencils. How could it include someone who has none?
packs.activity: Agree on a way to share an imaginary set fairly. Invite more than one reasonable solution.
packs.close: What is one detail that changed your idea?
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar discusses justice and good treatment. The pencil activity is editorial reflection, not a ruling on property.

passage.arabic: ۞ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِٱلْعَدْلِ وَٱلْإِحْسَـٰنِ وَإِيتَآئِ ذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَيَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ وَٱلْبَغْىِ ۚ يَعِظُكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ
passage.translation: Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed.

packs.title: Choose better words
packs.question: What kind of speech is requested in this reading?
packs.explanation: The passage asks Allah’s servants to speak in a better way.
packs.discussion: Two fictional teammates disagree about a rule. How could each state their view without insulting the other?
packs.activity: Offer two respectful versions of a made-up disagreement, then compare what each version makes clearer.
packs.close: Choose a useful opening sentence.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains good speech and the danger of discord. The conversation examples are editorial practice.

passage.arabic: وَقُل لِّعِبَادِى يَقُولُوا۟ ٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَـٰنَ يَنزَغُ بَيْنَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَـٰنَ كَانَ لِلْإِنسَـٰنِ عَدُوًّا مُّبِينًا
passage.translation: Tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier. Lo! the devil soweth discord among them. Lo! the devil is for man an open foe.

packs.title: Many peoples, one human family
packs.question: Why are peoples and tribes mentioned in the reading?
options: To require everyone to speak one language.
So people may know one another.
To prove that ancestry alone makes someone better.
packs.explanation: The passage mentions peoples and tribes and knowing one another.
packs.discussion: How can curiosity about another community avoid stereotypes? Use public examples rather than anyone’s private identity.
packs.activity: Invent three respectful questions about a public cultural tradition, and name where you would check the answers.
packs.close: Name one assumption you would want to check.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains shared human origin and rejects ancestry as the basis of superiority. The discussion questions are editorial reflection.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَـٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَـٰكُمْ شُعُوبًا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ
passage.translation: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware.

packs.title: A month begins
packs.question: What reason does the reading give for fasting being prescribed?
options: So that you may travel more easily.
So that you may ward off evil.
So that you may rest from every task.
packs.explanation: The passage ends with the reason: that you may ward off (evil). Al-Muyassar explains this as placing a protection between yourself and disobedience by obeying Allah.
packs.discussion: Doing without something for a day can help a person notice what they usually take for granted. What could that change in the way we treat other people? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Put an empty cup and a full cup side by side on the table. Each person names one good habit that fasting could help to build and moves a button from one cup to the other. Anyone may pass.
packs.close: Say one word you hope this month will build in you.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar says this verse speaks to believers and that fasting was prescribed for earlier communities too. Notice what the verse says about its purpose.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1903
sources.note: A report from Abu Hurairah: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says Allah has no need of someone giving up food and drink if that person does not also give up false speech and wrong actions. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ
passage.translation: O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil);

packs.title: A quiet moment
packs.question: What does the reading say Allah does when someone calls on Him?
options: He waits until a special day.
He is too far away to hear.
He answers the prayer of the one who calls.
packs.explanation: The passage says Allah is near and answers the prayer of the one who calls. Al-Muyassar adds that this nearness is the kind that suits Allah’s majesty.
packs.discussion: When might a person want to ask Allah for help? Think of made-up examples, and say how it feels to know He is near.
packs.activity: Pass a small cup from hand to hand. Whoever holds it may say a short dua aloud or silently, then pass it on. Anyone may pass.
packs.close: Say “Ameen” together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that this verse answers people who ask about Allah, and invites them to obey and believe so that they find the right way.

passage.arabic: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ ۖ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا۟ لِى وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا۟ بِى لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ
passage.translation: And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me. So let them hear My call and let them trust in Me, in order that they may be led aright.

packs.title: A message begins
packs.question: By what means does the reading say Allah teaches?
packs.explanation: The passage says Allah teaches by the pen and teaches people what they did not know. Al-Muyassar says He taught people to write with the pen and brought them from the darkness of not knowing to the light of knowledge. Surah 2, verse 185 names Ramadan as the month in which the Quran was revealed.
packs.discussion: The passage speaks of reading and of knowing what we did not know. What is something you have learned from a book or from someone who taught you? Use general examples if you prefer.
packs.activity: Put a pen, a sheet of paper and a closed book on the table. Each person chooses one object and says how it helps people learn. Then agree on one thing the family would like to learn together this month.
packs.close: Say one thing you would like to learn.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this as an instruction to read what was sent down, beginning with the name of the Lord who creates, and describes Him as most generous.

passage.arabic:
ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ
خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ
ٱقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْأَكْرَمُ
ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ
عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ
passage.translation:
Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth,
Createth man from a clot.
Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous,
Who teacheth by the pen,
Teacheth man that which he knew not.

packs.title: Open hands
packs.question: Who does the reading say should not be driven away?
options: The one who asks for help.
packs.explanation: The passage says the beggar should not be driven away. Al-Muyassar says to feed the one who asks, meet the need, and speak about the favours Allah has given you.
packs.discussion: Why is it kind to answer gently when someone asks for help? Think of made-up examples.
packs.activity: Pass a small bowl around. Each person pretends to put one kind thing in it by naming it, such as a smile, a hello or a seat. No real food or money is needed.
packs.close: Say thank you for one favour you have received. A thank-you is enough.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains these verses as three instructions about how to treat people and how to speak of Allah’s favours.

passage.arabic:
فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ
وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ
وَأَمَّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ
passage.translation:
Therefor the orphan oppress not,
Therefor the beggar drive not away,
Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.

packs.title: Counting thanks
packs.question: What does the reading say Allah will do if people give thanks?
packs.explanation: The passage says: If ye give thanks, I will give you more. Al-Muyassar says gratitude brings more of Allah’s favour. The verse also warns about being thankless, and an adult may explain that part gently.
packs.discussion: Besides words, what are some ways a person can show thanks? Which is hardest to remember?
packs.activity: Put five small objects in a row, such as a cup, a pen, a button, a spoon and a stone. Each person chooses one and says one thing it helps them do that they are thankful for.
packs.close: Say “Alhamdulillah” together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that Musa (peace be upon him) is reminding his people of what their Lord announced about thanks and thanklessness.

passage.arabic: وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ ۖ وَلَئِن كَفَرْتُمْ إِنَّ عَذَابِى لَشَدِيدٌ
passage.translation: And when your Lord proclaimed: If ye give thanks, I will give you more; but if ye are thankless, lo! My punishment is dire.

packs.title: Heavy and light
packs.question: What does the reading say goes together with hardship?
packs.explanation: The passage says that with hardship goes ease, and it says so twice. Al-Muyassar says harm from enemies should not hold the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ back from his message, because with a narrow time comes relief.
packs.discussion: Think of a made-up time when something was hard and then got easier. What helped?
packs.activity: Hold a stone in one hand and a feather or a tissue in the other. Say what feels heavy and what feels light, then swap hands and name one thing that makes a hard job easier.
packs.close: Say one thing that helps when something is hard.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this repeated verse as a comfort for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when others harmed him.

passage.arabic:
فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
إِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
passage.translation:
But lo! with hardship goeth ease,
Lo! with hardship goeth ease;

packs.title: Steady hearts
packs.question: What do the steadfast say when misfortune strikes them?
options: We are Allah’s and to Him we are returning.
packs.explanation: The passage says they say: Lo! we are Allah’s and lo! unto Him we are returning. Al-Muyassar explains that these words acknowledge that we belong to Allah and will return to Him, and that the steadfast are given glad tidings.
packs.discussion: Fasting brings a little hunger. How might patience with a small difficulty differ from patience with a large loss? Keep to made-up examples.
packs.activity: Set out three small objects: a cup for thirst, a plate for hunger and a stone for a hard moment. Take turns choosing one and say one steady response, either an action or a short phrase. Anyone may pass.
packs.close: Say one steady phrase you could remember.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar says Allah tests people with a little fear, hunger and loss, and gives good news to those who are patient.

passage.arabic:
وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَىْءٍ مِّنَ ٱلْخَوْفِ وَٱلْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ ٱلْأَمْوَٰلِ وَٱلْأَنفُسِ وَٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ ٱلصَّـٰبِرِينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَصَـٰبَتْهُم مُّصِيبَةٌ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
passage.translation:
And surely We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops; but give glad tidings to the steadfast,
Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.

packs.title: Small gifts
packs.question: What is spending in Allah’s way compared with in the reading?
options: A tree that gives shade once.
A grain that grows seven ears.
packs.explanation: The passage compares it to a grain that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each ear. Al-Muyassar says Allah multiplies the reward for whom He wills, according to the sincerity of the giver.
packs.discussion: How can a small gift grow into more good than the giver expected? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Use dry beans or other small objects. Each person puts one in a bowl and names one way a small gift can grow into more good. Count them together, then choose one real act of giving to talk over with an adult. No amounts need to be shared.
packs.close: Say one small gift you could give this week.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar describes spending in Allah’s way as among the most beneficial acts for believers. Using beans in the activity is an editorial aid.

passage.arabic: مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَٰلَهُمْ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أَنۢبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنَابِلَ فِى كُلِّ سُنۢبُلَةٍ مِّا۟ئَةُ حَبَّةٍ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ يُضَـٰعِفُ لِمَن يَشَآءُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ
passage.translation: The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. Allah giveth increase manifold to whom He will. Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing.

packs.title: Gentle words
packs.question: What does the reading say to ask Allah for?
packs.explanation: The passage is a dua: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little. Al-Muyassar adds that we should be humble and gentle with our parents and ask Allah to have mercy on them.
packs.discussion: Imagine a made-up family where a grown-up helps a child get ready for the day. What is one caring thing the grown-up could do, and what could the child say to thank them?
packs.activity: Stack small cups into a tower. Each person finishes the sentence “A caring thing a grown-up does is…” and adds one cup. Say the dua together when the tower is done.
packs.close: Say the dua together, or say thank you in your own words.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this verse as a call to gentle humility toward parents.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 5971
sources.note: A man asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ who most deserves his best company. The Prophet ﷺ answers “your mother” three times, then “your father”. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: وَٱخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ ٱلذُّلِّ مِنَ ٱلرَّحْمَةِ وَقُل رَّبِّ ٱرْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِى صَغِيرًا
passage.translation: And lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy, and say: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.

packs.title: Next door
packs.question: Which neighbours does the reading mention?
options: Only the neighbour who is a relative.
The neighbour who is related and the one who is not.
Only neighbours of the same age.
packs.explanation: The passage names the neighbour who is of kin and the neighbour who is not of kin. Al-Muyassar explains them as the near neighbour and the distant one.
packs.discussion: Why might a neighbour who is not a relative need kindness as much as a relative does? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Place several small cups in a row to stand for homes. Take turns moving a coin to a neighbouring cup and name one kind action toward a neighbour, such as a greeting, lowering noise or sharing something.
packs.close: Say one kind thing you could do for a neighbour.
packs.teaching: This verse is long and lists many people who deserve kindness, beginning with parents. An adult can skip the last phrase, which Al-Muyassar explains as those owned as servants, and focus on neighbours.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6014
sources.note: Aisha reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that Jibril kept advising him about the neighbour until he thought the neighbour might be made an heir. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: ۞ وَٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَلَا تُشْرِكُوا۟ بِهِۦ شَيْـًٔا ۖ وَبِٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ إِحْسَـٰنًا وَبِذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَٱلْيَتَـٰمَىٰ وَٱلْمَسَـٰكِينِ وَٱلْجَارِ ذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَٱلْجَارِ ٱلْجُنُبِ وَٱلصَّاحِبِ بِٱلْجَنۢبِ وَٱبْنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ وَمَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَـٰنُكُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ مَن كَانَ مُخْتَالًا فَخُورًا
passage.translation: And serve Allah. Ascribe no thing as partner unto Him. (Show) kindness unto parents, and unto near kindred, and orphans, and the needy, and unto the neighbour who is of kin (unto you) and the neighbour who is not of kin, and the fellow-traveller and the wayfarer and (the slaves) whom your right hands possess. Lo! Allah loveth not such as are proud and boastful,

packs.title: Keeping your word
packs.question: Whom does the reading say to be with?
packs.explanation: The passage says: be with the truthful. Al-Muyassar explains this as being with those who are truthful in their oaths, their promises and every matter.
packs.discussion: What is the difference between telling the truth and keeping a promise? Why do both build trust? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Put two cups on the table, one for “promised” and one for “kept”. Each person names a small made-up promise, puts a button in the first cup, then moves it to the second and says how it feels to keep a promise.
packs.close: Say one promise that is easy to keep this week.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this verse as an instruction to obey Allah and to keep a certain kind of company in promises and oaths.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6094
sources.note: Abdullah reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, while lying leads to wickedness. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَكُونُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلصَّـٰدِقِينَ
passage.translation: O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful.

packs.title: In the shade
packs.question: What did he say to his Lord?
options: I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.
I want to go home at once.
I am the strongest of all.
packs.explanation: The passage says he asked: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me. Al-Muyassar says this is Musa (peace be upon him), who had watered the flock for two women and was very hungry.
packs.discussion: He helped first and asked afterwards. Why might it be good to do a kindness before asking for something? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Put a cup of water and a small cloth on the table. The cloth stands for shade. Each person names one small way to help someone and one thing they could ask Allah for.
packs.close: Say one small way to help someone today.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that Musa (peace be upon him) gave water to two women and rested in the shade of a tree, and notes how hungry he was.

passage.arabic: فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّىٰٓ إِلَى ٱلظِّلِّ فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّى لِمَآ أَنزَلْتَ إِلَىَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ
passage.translation: So he watered (their flock) for them. Then he turned aside into the shade, and said: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me.

packs.title: Careful words
packs.question: What does the reading say is with a person for every word they say?
packs.explanation: The passage says there is an observer ready with every word. Al-Muyassar explains this as an angel who is present to watch and record the word.
packs.discussion: This verse reminds us to choose our words with care. What is one way to say something hard in a kind way? Use made-up sentences.
packs.activity: Hold a spoon and say a made-up sentence that could hurt someone. Then say a kinder way to say it and put the spoon down. Pass the spoon on.
packs.close: Say one kind sentence you could use today.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this verse as a reminder to speak with care.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018
sources.note: Abu Hurairah reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say what is good or stay quiet. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: مَّا يَلْفِظُ مِن قَوْلٍ إِلَّا لَدَيْهِ رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ
passage.translation: He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready.

packs.title: Before you assume
packs.question: Which of these does the reading say to avoid?
packs.explanation: The passage says to shun much suspicion, not to spy and not to backbite. Al-Muyassar explains that this means avoiding bad thoughts about believers, not searching for their faults and not saying behind someone’s back what they would dislike. People dislike the picture the verse gives, so they should dislike backbiting.
packs.discussion: Why can guessing about someone without checking be unfair? How can we choose a kinder explanation first? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: An adult secretly puts an ordinary object under a cup or in a closed box. Each person offers a guess, starting with the kindest guess they can think of. Then open it and talk about how guessing without knowing can be unfair.
packs.close: Say one kind assumption you could make today.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this verse as addressed to believers, ending with a reminder to be mindful of Allah, who accepts repentance and is merciful.

passage.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱجْتَنِبُوا۟ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِنَّ بَعْضَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ ۖ وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا ۚ أَيُحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن يَأْكُلَ لَحْمَ أَخِيهِ مَيْتًا فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ ۚ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَّحِيمٌ
passage.translation: O ye who believe! Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that (so abhor the other)! And keep your duty (to Allah). Lo! Allah is Relenting, Merciful.

packs.title: A gentle reply
packs.question: What does the speaker ask Allah to do?
packs.explanation: The passage says: May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy. Al-Muyassar says the speaker is Yusuf (peace be upon him) and that he tells his brothers there is no blame on them today.
packs.discussion: Why can it be hard to say “no blame today” after being hurt? What might help? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Put a small stone in a cup to stand for a hurt. Each person imagines a made-up hurt and says one forgiving sentence, then takes the stone out and puts it down beside the cup.
packs.close: Say one forgiving sentence you could use in a made-up case.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that Yusuf (peace be upon him) is speaking to his brothers.

passage.arabic: قَالَ لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْيَوْمَ ۖ يَغْفِرُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ ۖ وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
passage.translation: He said: Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.

packs.title: Calm replies
packs.question: How does the reading say to repel an evil deed?
packs.explanation: The passage says: Repel the evil deed with one which is better. Al-Muyassar explains this as answering harm with forgiveness, patience and kindness, and says only those who are patient are given this quality.
packs.discussion: What does it take to answer a rude word with a calm one? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Put two cups on the table, one for “harsh” and one for “better”. An adult reads a made-up unkind remark. Each person offers a calm reply and moves a button to the second cup.
packs.close: Say one calm reply you could use.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this verse as guidance on how to respond to someone who has harmed you.

passage.arabic: وَلَا تَسْتَوِى ٱلْحَسَنَةُ وَلَا ٱلسَّيِّئَةُ ۚ ٱدْفَعْ بِٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ فَإِذَا ٱلَّذِى بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُۥ عَدَٰوَةٌ كَأَنَّهُۥ وَلِىٌّ حَمِيمٌ
passage.translation: The good deed and the evil deed are not alike. Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend.

packs.title: Two builders
packs.question: What were they doing when they prayed?
options: Raising the foundations of the House.
packs.explanation: The passage says Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House. Al-Muyassar explains this as the Kaaba, and says they prayed humbly that Allah accept their work.
packs.discussion: They asked Allah to accept their work as they built. Why might a person ask for acceptance after doing a good deed?
packs.activity: Stack small blocks or cups to build together. Before each one is placed, the person says one good deed they could try, and everyone says “Our Lord, accept from us.”
packs.close: Say “Our Lord, accept from us” together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this as a prayer by Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and Ismail (peace be upon him) as they worked, calling on Allah humbly.

passage.arabic:
وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَـٰعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
رَبَّنَا وَٱجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةً مُّسْلِمَةً لَّكَ وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا وَتُبْ عَلَيْنَآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
passage.translation:
And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, (Abraham prayed): Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.
Our Lord! And make us submissive unto Thee and of our seed a nation submissive unto Thee, and show us our ways of worship, and relent toward us. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Relenting, the Merciful.

packs.title: Out of the dark
packs.question: What did he say when he cried out?
options: There is no god but You. Glory to You. I was a wrong-doer.
packs.explanation: The passage says he cried out: There is no Allah save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer. Al-Muyassar says this was Yunus (peace be upon him), who admitted his fault, and that Allah answered him and rescued him.
packs.discussion: He admitted his mistake and called on Allah. Why can it be hard to say “I was wrong”? What does it make easier?
packs.activity: Dim the room a little if that is safe. Hold a torch under a cloth. Each person says the words from the reading or a short dua of their own. Then lift the cloth to let the light shine.
packs.close: Say one short dua you could use when something goes wrong.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that Yunus (peace be upon him) was tested with distress and called on Allah from the dark.

passage.arabic:
وَذَا ٱلنُّونِ إِذ ذَّهَبَ مُغَـٰضِبًا فَظَنَّ أَن لَّن نَّقْدِرَ عَلَيْهِ فَنَادَىٰ فِى ٱلظُّلُمَـٰتِ أَن لَّآ إِلَـٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبْحَـٰنَكَ إِنِّى كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ
فَٱسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُۥ وَنَجَّيْنَـٰهُ مِنَ ٱلْغَمِّ ۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُـۨجِى ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
passage.translation:
And (mention) Dhu'n-Nun, when he went off in anger and deemed that We had no power over him, but he cried out in the darkness, saying: There is no Allah save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer.
Then we heard his prayer and saved him from the anguish. Thus we save believers.

packs.title: A prayer before speaking
packs.question: What did he ask for, so that people would understand him?
options: A knot loosened from his tongue.
packs.explanation: The passage says he asked Allah to loose a knot from his tongue so that they may understand his words. Al-Muyassar says this is Musa (peace be upon him), who also asked for his brother Harun (peace be upon him) as a helper.
packs.discussion: Have you ever wanted to say something clearly and found it hard? What could help? Use made-up examples if you prefer.
packs.activity: Tie a loose knot in a piece of string or a scarf. Take turns gently untying it while saying: “My Lord, ease my task for me.”
packs.close: Say one thing you want to say clearly this week.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this as the prayer of Musa (peace be upon him) before a hard task.

passage.arabic:
قَالَ رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى
وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى
وَٱحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِى
يَفْقَهُوا۟ قَوْلِى
passage.translation:
(Moses) said: My Lord! relieve my mind
And ease my task for me;
And loose a knot from my tongue,
That they may understand my saying.

packs.title: A call from hardship
packs.question: What does the reading say happened after his prayer?
options: He travelled to a new land.
The adversity was removed and he was given his household and the like with them.
packs.explanation: The passage says Allah heard his prayer, removed the adversity and gave him his household and the like of it, as a mercy and a reminder. Al-Muyassar says this is Ayyub (peace be upon him), who was patient through illness and loss and called on his Lord.
packs.discussion: He praised Allah as the Most Merciful before asking. How might remembering Allah’s mercy change the way we ask?
packs.activity: Fold a cloth into a blanket. Each person says a short dua for someone who is going through illness or hardship, without naming anyone private, and lays a button on the cloth.
packs.close: Say one dua for someone who is going through a hard time.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that Ayyub (peace be upon him) was tested with illness and with the loss of family and wealth, was patient, and called on his Lord.

passage.arabic:
۞ وَأَيُّوبَ إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥٓ أَنِّى مَسَّنِىَ ٱلضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرْحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
فَٱسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُۥ فَكَشَفْنَا مَا بِهِۦ مِن ضُرٍّ ۖ وَءَاتَيْنَـٰهُ أَهْلَهُۥ وَمِثْلَهُم مَّعَهُمْ رَحْمَةً مِّنْ عِندِنَا وَذِكْرَىٰ لِلْعَـٰبِدِينَ
passage.translation:
And Job, when he cried unto his Lord, (saying): Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy.
Then We heard his prayer and removed that adversity from which he suffered, and We gave him his household (that he had lost) and the like thereof along with them, a mercy from Our store, and a remembrance for the worshippers;

packs.title: A blessed night
packs.question: What does the reading say happened on the blessed night?
packs.explanation: The passage says: We revealed it on a blessed night. Al-Muyassar explains this as the Quran being sent down on the blessed Night of Qadr, which it says is in Ramadan, a night in which every wise command is made clear.
packs.discussion: The last ten nights are a time many people try to do more. What is one realistic thing a family could change in these nights?
packs.activity: Put a lamp or torch, a book and a prayer mat on the table. Each person chooses the object that matches one thing they would like to do in the last ten nights and says why. Then agree on one small plan together.
packs.close: Say the one plan you chose.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar names the night this verse speaks of and says what is made clear in it.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2024
sources.note: Aisha reports that when the last ten days of Ramadan began, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would work hard, spend the night in prayer and wake his family. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic:
إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَـٰهُ فِى لَيْلَةٍ مُّبَـٰرَكَةٍ ۚ إِنَّا كُنَّا مُنذِرِينَ
فِيهَا يُفْرَقُ كُلُّ أَمْرٍ حَكِيمٍ
passage.translation:
Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night - Lo! We are ever warning -
Whereon every wise command is made clear

packs.title: After a mistake
packs.question: What do they ask Allah for in the reading?
packs.explanation: The passage says: If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost. Al-Muyassar says these are the words Adam (peace be upon him) received from his Lord and called on, and that Allah accepted his repentance.
packs.discussion: Everyone makes mistakes. What can we do when we have made one? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Hold an empty cup in open hands. Each person says softly, “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. Forgive us and have mercy on us.” Then pour a little water into a bowl to stand for a worry being washed away.
packs.close: Say “Ameen” together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this as Adam and Hawwa speaking to their Lord after their mistake.

sources.label: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 3513
sources.note: Aisha asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ what to say if she knows the Night of Qadr. He teaches a short dua asking Allah, who loves pardon, to pardon her. Graded Sahih (Darussalam) on sunnah.com. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic: قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَـٰسِرِينَ
passage.translation: They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!

packs.title: Quiet hours
packs.question: What does the reading say they did before each dawn?
packs.explanation: The passage says they slept little of the night and before dawn sought forgiveness. Al-Muyassar says they prayed to their Lord and asked forgiveness for their sins in the last part of the night.
packs.discussion: What might a family do in the quiet part of a night that is hard to do in the day? Think of ideas, not private stories.
packs.activity: Lay out three objects in the order of a night: a cushion, a prayer mat and a cup. Put them in order and say what each person could do with each one in the last ten nights. Agree on one small step.
packs.close: Say one quiet thing you could do tonight.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this as describing people who do good and what they do at night.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2014
sources.note: Abu Hurairah reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Qadr out of faith and hoping for Allah’s reward will have past sins forgiven. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic:
كَانُوا۟ قَلِيلًا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ مَا يَهْجَعُونَ
وَبِٱلْأَسْحَارِ هُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ
passage.translation:
They used to sleep but little of the night,
And ere the dawning of each day would seek forgiveness,

packs.title: Hurrying to good
packs.question: Which of these is among those described in the reading?
options: Those who control their wrath and are forgiving.
Those who keep every gift for themselves.
packs.explanation: The passage describes those who spend in ease and hardship, control their wrath and are forgiving toward people. Al-Muyassar explains this as spending, holding back anger with patience and pardoning those who wronged them, which it calls the excellence that Allah loves.
packs.discussion: Why is forgiving harder when we are angry? Which step comes first: calming down or forgiving? Use made-up examples.
packs.activity: Fill a cup to the brim with water. Each person says one thing they can do when angry, such as pause, breathe or walk away, and carefully carries the full cup across the room without spilling.
packs.close: Say one thing you can do when you feel angry.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that this passage calls believers to hurry toward their Lord’s forgiveness, and says Allah loves those it describes.

passage.arabic:
۞ وَسَارِعُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ فِى ٱلسَّرَّآءِ وَٱلضَّرَّآءِ وَٱلْكَـٰظِمِينَ ٱلْغَيْظَ وَٱلْعَافِينَ عَنِ ٱلنَّاسِ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ
passage.translation:
And vie one with another for forgiveness from your Lord, and for a paradise as wide as are the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who ward off (evil);
Those who spend (of that which Allah hath given them) in ease and in adversity, those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind; Allah loveth the good;

packs.title: A shared meal
packs.question: Why do they say they feed others?
options: For the sake of Allah only.
packs.explanation: The passage says they feed others for the sake of Allah only and wish for no reward or thanks. Al-Muyassar names the people they feed as the poor, the orphan and the captive.
packs.discussion: Why might giving without asking for thanks feel different? What can the person who receives do to say thank you?
packs.activity: Set out empty plates and cups. Each person “prepares” a plate by placing a button on it and says who it could be shared with in general terms. Then talk with an adult about one real act of sharing.
packs.close: Say one way to give without expecting thanks.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains these verses as describing people who feed others, and says whom they feed.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1902
sources.note: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was the most generous of people, and most generous in Ramadan, when Jibril met him each night and the Prophet ﷺ recited the Quran to him. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic:
وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا
إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمْ جَزَآءً وَلَا شُكُورًا
passage.translation:
And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him,
(Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you;

packs.title: Four short lines
packs.question: How does the reading describe Allah at the start?
options: He is a king of one city.
packs.explanation: The passage begins: Say: He is Allah, the One! Al-Muyassar explains that He alone is God and Lord, with no partner, and that all creatures turn to Him for their needs.
packs.discussion: This surah is short and easy to learn. Why might a short surah be a good one to learn first? Is there one you know?
packs.activity: Put four small objects in a row, one for each line. Say the lines together and touch one object for each. Then each person reads a line alone, or passes.
packs.close: Say the first line together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains this short surah as a description of Allah.

passage.arabic:
قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ
ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ
لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ
وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌۢ
passage.translation:
Say: He is Allah, the One!
Allah, the eternally Besought of all!
He begetteth not nor was begotten.
And there is none comparable unto Him.

packs.title: The Night of Power
packs.question: What is the Night of Power better than?
packs.explanation: The passage says the Night of Power is better than a thousand months. Al-Muyassar says doing good in it is better than the good done in a thousand months without such a night, that the angels and Jibril descend, and that it is peace until dawn. The start of Ramadan depends on moon sighting, so this pack does not say which night is the Night of Power.
packs.discussion: Why do you think people try to be kind and to pray more in this night? What is one small kind thing you could do?
packs.activity: Place a jar and a bowl of beans on the table. Each person adds one bean to the jar for one kind thing they will try tonight. Look at the jar and talk about how small good deeds can add up.
packs.close: Say a short dua together, or say “Ameen”.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains that the Quran was sent down on the noble Night of Qadr, one of the nights of Ramadan, and that it is peace until dawn.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 2017
sources.note: Aisha reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying to search for the Night of Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan. Paraphrased.

passage.arabic:
إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَـٰهُ فِى لَيْلَةِ ٱلْقَدْرِ
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا لَيْلَةُ ٱلْقَدْرِ
لَيْلَةُ ٱلْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِّنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ
تَنَزَّلُ ٱلْمَلَـٰٓئِكَةُ وَٱلرُّوحُ فِيهَا بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِم مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ
سَلَـٰمٌ هِىَ حَتَّىٰ مَطْلَعِ ٱلْفَجْرِ
passage.translation:
Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Predestination.
Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is!
The Night of Power is better than a thousand months.
The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by the permission of their Lord, with all decrees.
(The night is) Peace until the rising of the dawn.

packs.title: Growing well
packs.question: What does the successful person do after remembering the name of their Lord?
packs.explanation: The passage says the successful person grows, remembers the name of their Lord and prays. Al-Muyassar explains this as purifying oneself from bad character, remembering Allah and praying on time. The abridged English Ibn Kathir reports that Umar bin Abdul-Aziz used to command people to give sadaqat al-fitr and would recite this verse.
packs.discussion: The commentary links these verses with giving before the Eid prayer. Why might giving before prayer matter? What might it mean to “purify” character?
packs.activity: Put a small cup on the table to stand for a measure. Each person says one thing that could “grow” in character. Then agree to ask a knowledgeable adult how zakat al-fitr is given where you live. This pack does not set amounts.
packs.close: Say one thing you want to grow in.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains these verses as describing the person who succeeds. The abridged English Ibn Kathir mentions Umar bin Abdul-Aziz reciting them when commanding sadaqat al-fitr.

sources.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 1503
sources.note: Ibn Umar reports the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made zakat al-fitr obligatory: a measure of dates or barley on every Muslim, young or old, to be paid before people go out to the Eid prayer. Paraphrased.

sources.label: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged, English) on 87:14-15
sources.note: Mentions Umar bin Abdul-Aziz reciting this verse when commanding sadaqat al-fitr.

passage.arabic:
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ
وَذَكَرَ ٱسْمَ رَبِّهِۦ فَصَلَّىٰ
passage.translation:
He is successful who groweth,
And remembereth the name of his Lord, so prayeth,

packs.title: Throughout the day
packs.question: When does the reading say to glorify Allah?
packs.explanation: The passage says to glorify Him early and late, and to remember Allah with much remembrance. Al-Muyassar says this includes morning and evening and after the prayers.
packs.discussion: Which short words of remembrance do you know? When could we say them in a day?
packs.activity: Put a cup and ten beans on the table. Each time someone says “SubhanAllah” or “Alhamdulillah”, they move a bean into the cup. Count to ten together.
packs.close: Say “Alhamdulillah” together.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar explains these verses as a call to remember Allah often, with the heart, the tongue and actions.

passage.arabic:
يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱذْكُرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ذِكْرًا كَثِيرًا
وَسَبِّحُوهُ بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا
passage.translation:
O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance.
And glorify Him early and late.

packs.title: The month’s end
packs.question: What does the reading say Allah desires for you?
packs.explanation: The passage says Allah desires ease for you and not hardship. Al-Muyassar adds that the month is completed, that Allah is magnified for guiding us with the takbir at Eid al-Fitr, and that we give thanks.
packs.discussion: As the month ends, what is one thing you will remember with thanks? Keep your answer general if you prefer.
packs.activity: Put 30 beans in a jar. Pass it around and take one out each time a person names a good thing they remember from the month, in general terms. Then ask a knowledgeable adult for the takbir words your family uses.
packs.close: Say one thing you are thankful for from this month.
packs.teaching: Al-Muyassar connects this verse with Ramadan, fasting, the end of the month and Eid al-Fitr.

passage.arabic: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَـٰتٍ مِّنَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ وَٱلْفُرْقَانِ ۚ فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ ٱلشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ ۖ وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِّنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ ۗ يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ وَلِتُكْمِلُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ وَلِتُكَبِّرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمْ وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ
passage.translation: The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion (of right and wrong). And whosoever of you is present, let him fast the month, and whosoever of you is sick or on a journey, (let him fast the same) number of other days. Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you; and (He desireth) that ye should complete the period, and that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful.

methodology: Twelve single-sitting family packs combine a source reading question, an open discussion and a shared activity. Age bands are editorial suggestions and Pickthall’s historical English may need an adult’s explanation. Open prompts have no single graded answer. Activities are original applications beyond the fetched canonical text, not scholarly rulings from quran.ai, quran.com or quran.foundation. No child names, private stories, profiles or ongoing behavior records are collected. Every participant may pass.
